title: IP rating chart: Specifying and verifying ingress protection
summary: IP rating chart plus how to specify, test, and hold an IP67 enclosure in production: drawing callouts, verification, and supplier control.
body_markdown:
Under IEC 60529, IP67 means dust-tight (IP6X) and protected during 30 minutes of immersion with the enclosure’s lowest point 1,000 mm below the surface. A slightly warped lid, a cable gland loaded outside its approved cable range, a connector swapped after qualification. Any one of these can open the leak path that a dimensional inspection would never catch.


The IP code itself isn’t the hard part. Holding that rating through a production run is.


[IEC 60529](https://webstore.iec.ch/en/publication/2447) defines the ingress protection classification: a first digit for protection against solid objects and dust, a second for protection against water under specified test conditions. The code tells you what was tested – not how a supplier should build the enclosure so every unit off the line keeps meeting it. For that, the requirement has to reach the drawing, the gasket design, the sealing surfaces, every penetration, the manufacturing process, the acceptance plan, and revision control. The enclosure is only as tight as its lowest-rated penetration, and a port left without its cover falls outside the rating.


The IP rating system defines intrusion resilience for solids and liquids as the first and second figures


There are a few things the chart alone won’t tell you. An X in an IP code doesn’t mean zero protection – it means that characteristic wasn’t specified. IPX7 specifies the immersion test and makes no claim at all about solid-particle protection. Specify the first digit whenever dust matters: passing a water test does not prove an enclosure is dust-tight.


The water column also isn’t a simple ladder where each higher number includes every test below it. Immersion and jet testing stress an enclosure’s seals in different ways. A part that passes IPX7 immersion has passed that test only. It hasn’t been shown to meet IPX5 or IPX6 jet testing by extension. If a product will realistically see both conditions, both need to be specified and verified on their own terms.


## What IP67 means for a sealed enclosure


IP67 pairs the top dust rating, IP6X, with the IPX7 temporary-immersion test. For an enclosure under 850 mm tall, that test places the lowest point 1,000 mm below the water surface for 30 minutes. That is a specific, bounded test condition, not a general claim of “waterproof.”


An IP67 pass says nothing about resistance to powerful jets, prolonged deep immersion, steam cleaning, chemical exposure, or pressure washing. Any of those that are realistic in service need their own line item in the environmental requirements, tested separately.


The IP rating system defines intrusion resilience for solids and liquids as the first and second figures.


IP68 is a different thing again – continuous immersion under conditions the manufacturer and customer agree on is considerably more severe than IPX7, by design. Without knowing the agreed depth, duration, and other conditions, an IP68 callout on its own doesn’t carry much engineering meaning.


At the far end of the water-exposure spectrum, IP69 and the automotive IP6K9K classification under


[ISO 20653](https://www.iso.org/standard/76116.html) cover close-range, high-pressure, high-temperature jets – a load profile that has almost nothing in common with static immersion. A product that sees rain, washdown, submersion, and hot pressure-washing over its life may need more than one qualification, not one rating stretched to cover all of it.


## How to specify an IP rating on an engineering drawing


A drawing note like “Ingress protection: IP67 per IEC 60529” sets the test target, but it doesn’t define the enclosure configuration that has to pass it.


The controlled spec needs to pin down exactly what’s under test. Are the cable glands installed with cables in them? Are unused ports plugged? Are connector caps fitted or removed? Is the service cover closed? What orientation is used? Are vents installed, and which gasket revision is on the part?


Ingress protection is a property of the assembled configuration. A machined body doesn’t carry IP67 by itself; the rating belongs to the housing plus its lid, gasket, fasteners, connectors, and every penetration together. Which means your supplier can deliver a housing that conforms to print while your finished assembly still fails its ingress test, because the gap was never in the machining.


### Sealing-surface geometry


Flatness across a lid or flange often matters more than might be obvious. A machined surface can sit inside its thickness tolerance and still distort just enough to reduce gasket compression locally – on larger enclosures in particular, the region between fasteners bows slightly while the areas right around each screw stay clamped tight.


Surface finish carries its own risks. Deeper machining marks, scratches, porosity, or local handling damage on a sealing surface can open a leak path, even when the flatness looks fine at inspection.


There’s no universal IP67 flatness or finish tolerance that works across designs – the right value arises from experience with the seal design, enclosure stiffness, gasket material, pressure differential, and manufacturing process together. It must be derived from the joint, not copied from a different product’s drawing.


Fastener position and spacing belong in that same analysis. Cranking up clamp load at one screw does almost nothing for a section of gasket sitting under-compressed halfway to the next one – lid stiffness, flange stiffness, gasket reaction force, and fastener spacing all interact. This is why a sealing failure caught at final IP testing costs you scrapped parts and a repeat qualification:


### Gasket selection and compression


The gasket spec needs to name the exact material and geometry that was qualified – not an generic equivalent. Compression is the variable that does the most damage in either direction. Too little leaves gaps or weak contact pressure; too much can permanently set some cellular materials, raise closure loads unnecessarily, and eat into the gasket’s ability to absorb dimensional variation and thermal cycling later.


Groove geometry decides where the gasket goes once it’s compressed, so width, depth, corner radii, and cross-section all need to be worked out together rather than as defaults.


Material behavior adds a time dimension most static tests don’t capture. Elastomers change with temperature and age, oils and cleaners. Even UV exposure can shift their properties, and compression set can reduce sealing force over years of service. A design that passes a new-build IP test hasn’t been shown to hold the same sealing performance after thermal cycling and environmental exposure – those are two different questions, and passing one doesn’t answer the other.


A wide variety of methods and materials are used in creating IP resilience. In the injection molded box example we refer to in this article, an O-ring sits in a groove at the box rim and meets a rib on the lid that is pressed against it by the fasteners and the overall stiffness of the parts. The compression deforms the O-ring and creates the seal.


## Every penetration is part of the enclosure


Cable glands, connectors, pushbuttons, displays, vents, pressure-equalization devices, and removable plugs all break the enclosure boundary, and each one needs its own environmental capability installed within the exact conditions that capability was qualified under.


A cable gland is a clean example. Its sealing performance depends on cable diameter, gland size, thread engagement, the sealing washer, installation torque, and cable construction – swap in a slightly smaller cable because it happens to fit through the gland, and the assembly has moved outside the configuration the gland was qualified for.


Connectors carry the same risk in a different shape. A connector’s ingress rating can be entirely different depending on whether it’s mated, unmated, or fitted with its protective cap. Ask whether the connector is IP67 in the exact state you build and use it in: mated, unmated, or capped.


## Holding IP67 in CNC-machined enclosures


Machined enclosures give you direct control over sealing landings, grooves, threaded penetrations, and mating geometry, which makes them a strong fit for tightly controlled sealed assemblies, as long as your drawing spells out which dimensions matter to the seal.


A lid recess might carry a generous general depth tolerance everywhere except the gasket groove, which needs much tighter control. External cosmetic surfaces can tolerate ordinary milling marks; the sealing land can’t, and needs a defined finish plus protection from handling damage on the way to assembly.


Flatness callouts should tie directly to the gasketed joint. On parts with substantial material removal, thin walls, or asymmetric machining, the part can move after it’s unclamped – a sealing surface that measured flat while heavily restrained on the machine may not hold that geometry once it’s free. Inspection needs to reproduce the condition the drawing requirement applies to, not just the condition that’s easiest to fixture.


Threads and tapped holes deserve a second look wherever they cross the enclosure boundary. A screw into a blind boss that never communicates with the protected volume is a completely different sealing problem from a fastener hole that opens straight into the enclosure interior. Decide which one you have during design, before immersion testing.


## Holding ingress protection in sheet-metal enclosures


Sheet metal runs a different tolerance chain. Bent panels can distort, welded seams can shrink or warp, large removable covers can deflect between fasteners, and a flange that reads as continuous on the drawing can carry local steps at corners or welded joints in reality.


Where a weld forms part of the enclosure boundary, weld integrity becomes an ingress-control item in its own right, not just a structural one. Bolted or riveted seams shift more of the burden onto gasket and flange geometry instead – the design needs enough local stiffness and fastener distribution to hold gasket compression around the full perimeter, corners included.


A leak at a sheet-metal corner can trace back to the seal, flange distortion, weld condition, fastener spacing, or some combination of them. Swapping the gasket without finding the actual physical leak path can make a part pass its next test, while leaving the underlying process just as unstable as before.


### Holding IP ratings in injection-molded enclosures


For molded parts, sealing decisions need to be locked in before tooling gets cut. Parting lines, draft, ejector positions, gate strategy, screw bosses, inserts, wall thickness, and expected molding distortion all interact with sealing geometry – a gasket groove that models cleanly in CAD can turn out difficult to hold consistently once shrinkage and warpage enter the picture.


The sealing land and groove should be reviewed as functional features during tooling design, not treated as generic geometry that will sort itself out. This matters most on a long rectangular cover that depends on uniform compression around its perimeter, where small local dimensional shifts accumulate and screw-boss placement determines where clamp load enters the molded structure. If you find out the joint is sensitive to normal molding variation only after samples fail immersion testing, you’re paying for re-cut tooling and a repeat qualification.


IP rating does not presuppose a manufacture method for an enclosure - all options are practical, though each poses its own challenges.


## IP verification is performed on the configuration you ship


An IEC 60529 pass is a type test on new parts. It says nothing about seal performance after aging or thermal cycling. Ingress protection gets established through testing, which means the configuration under test matters at least as much as the nominal IP code stamped on the drawing. The test article needs to represent the real product build – seals, covers, cable entries, connectors, and every other relevant penetration exactly as they’ll ship. Prototype testing validates the design. Certification requires testing the production configuration.


Temperature is part of that too. A hot enclosure immersed in colder water can cool internally, which drops internal pressure and pulls water toward any available leakage path. Test procedures control the temperature difference between specimen and water for exactly this reason; Infinita Lab’s IP testing guidance keeps the water within 5 °C of the device temperature for this reason” It’s also why an enclosure can behave very differently in the field than it does in a casual room-temperature bucket test.


An accredited lab can run the standardized qualification test and document both the configuration and the result, and that report should become part of the controlled product record. That still leaves the separate question of production acceptance – testing every unit to the full IEC type-test sequence is often impractical, so many programs instead rely on controlled manufacturing processes combined with dimensional inspection, leak testing, sampling, or another acceptance method correlated back to the qualified design.


Which method makes sense depends on product risk, production volume, customer requirements, and how costly a leak failure would be downstream. Whatever gets chosen needs to be defined before production starts, a PO that just says “must be IP67” without specifying what evidence acceptance requires leaves acceptance up to your supplier’s judgment.


## Why IP67 enclosures fail


A leak almost always has an identifiable physical path. On gasketed covers, uneven compression is usually the first thing worth measuring, check the sealing geometry and compression around the full perimeter before assuming that tightening the screws further will fix anything.


Warped covers and flanges create local low-pressure regions in the gasket. Surface damage opens a narrow leak channel. Wrong groove depth leaves a gasket under-compressed even when the assembly looks fully closed from the outside. Fastener holes and threaded penetrations leak if they communicate with the protected volume at all.


Cable glands fail when the installed cable diameter sits outside the specified sealing range. Connectors may only have been qualified mated or capped, not in whatever state the field uses them. Vents can be installed wrong, or swapped for a part that looks similar but carries different environmental characteristics.


Pressure differential deserves its own attention. Temperature swings can repeatedly push air through small openings, and a pressure-equalization vent can relieve that load – but the vent itself then becomes part of the environmental boundary and nso include it in the tested configuration.


One of the more troublesome production failures happens when nothing obviously changes on the enclosure. Someone swaps a gasket supplier, a connector, a coating thickness, a machining process, a fastener, or a gland, the assembly drawing number stays the same, or the revision bump looks minor, and nobody flags another ingress review. The original test report is still sitting in the file. It just no longer describes the part that’s shipping. This is where spreadsheet-and-email supplier management breaks down. The substitution lives in one supplier’s inbox, and nobody connects it to the ingress review.


## IP ratings belong inside the production quality system


AS9102 FAI sits inside an AS9100 quality system, so it asks for AS9100 (or ISO 9001) certification from every supplier in the chain. Once an enclosure clears qualification, the job shifts to keeping every subsequent unit inside that validated configuration and process window – starting with drawing and BOM revision control. The gasket spec, critical sealing geometry, connectors, glands, plugs, and other environmental-boundary components all need to be individually identifiable, and any supplier substitution that could touch ingress performance needs engineering review before it happens, not after.


A first article inspection establishes that the production process can reproduce the defined geometry. Where


[AS9102](https://www.sae.org/standards/content/as9102c/) applies contractually, FAI gives a structured record tying drawing characteristics to measured inspection results. Production programs may layer


[PPAP](https://www.aiag.org/quality) or a customer-specific approval system on top, covering the manufacturing process, measurement methods, material controls, and change management.


Material certs and lot traceability matter most when a seal or component turns out to be defective later.” If a gasket material, gland batch, or machining process changes, you need to know which finished assemblies contain it before the next shipment goes out.


The certificate of conformance sits at the end of a much longer evidence chain:


**Released configuration → controlled materials and components → manufactured enclosure → dimensional and process verification → qualified ingress test → production acceptance → traceable shipped assembly**


That chain is what lets an IP requirement mean something past the original test samples, rather than expiring the moment production starts making changes nobody flagged.


## When does an enclosure need to be retested?


Any change that could touch the ingress boundary should trigger an engineering review, though that doesn’t mean every drawing revision needs a full external lab requalification. Moving an internal mounting boss, for instance, may have zero effect on the enclosure boundary at all.


Changing gasket material is a high risk difference. So is modifying a sealing groove, changing lid material or thickness, relocating fasteners, altering a connector, substituting a cable gland, changing a vent, revising a welded seam, moving an injection-mold parting line, or changing a manufacturing process that affects sealing-surface geometry. The engineering review is what decides whether existing test evidence still applies or whether some level of re-verification is needed, and that decision is much easier to make well when the original test report clearly documents the tested configuration in the first place. A certificate that lists only a model number and “IP67 PASS” gives almost nothing to work with several revisions down the road.


## NEMA and IP are not equivalent systems


NEMA enclosure types and IEC IP codes overlap on some environmental protection but aren’t interchangeable classifications.


[NEMA 250](https://www.nema.org/docs/default-source/standards-document-library/ansi_nema_250-2020-contents-and-scope76f809d7-afad-4aa1-80cd-e1d09b60f2e5.pdf?sfvrsn=cb4086bd_3) covers additional conditions the two IP digits don’t capture at all, corrosion, icing, and oil resistance among them, depending on enclosure type.


Comparison tables between the two systems only run in one direction. A NEMA type may meet or exceed a stated IP classification, but an enclosure carrying that IP classification can’t automatically be claimed to satisfy the equivalent NEMA type; the logic doesn’t reverse. That distinction matters on drawings and customer specs specifically because swapping a required NEMA type for the closest-looking IP number can silently drop requirements nobody meant to drop.


## IK and IP protect against other factors than fluid ingress


The IK code, defined in


[IEC 62262](https://webstore.iec.ch/publication/6673) , covers mechanical impact resistance; a completely separate concern from ingress protection. The scale runs from IK00 (no protection) to IK10 (20 J), and Amendment 1:2021 added IK11 (50 J). Each step is defined by a specific impact energy and test geometry.


An enclosure can carry both an IP rating and an IK rating at once precisely because the two answer different questions: IP tells you about access, solids, and water under defined tests; IK tells you about resistance to a defined mechanical impact. Neither can be inferred from the other, and a high IP number says nothing about how the enclosure holds up to a dropped tool or a stray impact.


The same logic applies to the automotive-specific classifications under ISO 20653/2023.


[IP6K9K](https://i-pro.com/products_and_solutions/en/surveillance/weather-resistant) , for instance, addresses dust protection and high-pressure, high-temperature water exposure under that particular system, it belongs on a spec where that exact test reflects a real product requirement, not as a generic stand-in for “tougher than IP67.”

## Supplier approval checklist for an IP-rated enclosure


Before you release an enclosure for production, confirm:


- The required IP classification and applicable standard are stated.


- The exact tested assembly configuration is defined.


- The gasket material and cross-section are controlled.


- Gasket groove geometry and relevant sealing dimensions are tolerance.


- Sealing-surface flatness and finish requirements are defined where needed.


- Fastener size, location, and assembly requirements preserve the intended gasket compression.


- Every penetration through the environmental boundary has been identified.


- Cable glands are used within their specified cable range and installation conditions.


- Connector environmental ratings apply to the actual mated, unmated, or capped state.


- Vents and plugs are included in the controlled configuration.


- Welded seams forming part of the enclosure boundary have defined workmanship or acceptance requirements.


- The test configuration, orientation, and relevant environmental conditions are documented.


- Qualification reports identify the tested revision.


- Production inspection and sampling requirements are written into the drawing, spec, or purchase order.


- Material and component traceability requirements are established where appropriate.


- FAI, PPAP, or customer-specific production approval requirements are defined.


- A change to a gasket, sealing surface, penetration, connector, gland, vent, or relevant manufacturing process triggers engineering review.


- Responsibility for re-verification after a significant change is agreed before production begins.


If you’re working across several processes and specialist suppliers, this is exactly where a manufacturing arm earns its role. The CNC shop controls the sealing land, another supplier makes the gasket, connectors come off a catalog manufacturer’s shelf, and an independent lab runs qualification – someone still has to own the released configuration and confirm the parts reaching production match what was tested. Jiga is that supplier of records. You keep direct access to the qualified shops making each part, and your Jiga team delivers the evidence chain: FAI (AS9102 on A&D programs), CoCs, material certs, and lot traceability, with PPAP on production. Audit rights and AVL control stay with you


## Frequently Asked Questions


What does IP67 mean for an enclosure?


IP67 means the enclosure is dust-tight (IP6X) and has passed the IPX7 temporary-immersion test, for the applicable enclosure size, that’s the lowest point sitting 1,000 mm below the water surface for 30 minutes. What it doesn’t cover is everything else water can do to a product: jetting, prolonged immersion, and high-pressure hot-water cleaning are all separate test conditions under separate codes water jets (IPX5 and IPX6), continuous immersion (IPX8), and high-pressure hot-water cleaning (IPX9 or IP69K) are separate tests under separate codes, and passing one doesn’t imply passing the others. If a product will realistically encounter more than one of those exposures, treat it as more than one requirement.


What is the difference between IP67 and IP68?


IP67 specifies temporary immersion under fixed conditions, a set depth for a set duration. IP68 covers continuous immersion, but under conditions the manufacturer and customer agree on rather than a fixed universal test, which means an IP68 callout is only as useful as the depth, duration, and other conditions attached to it. Without those specifics, “IP68” functions more as a category than a testable requirement.


Does IP67 mean waterproof, and does it resist water jets?


No, on both counts. IP67 confirms a pass on specific dust and temporary-immersion tests; nothing more. It says nothing about the IPX5 or IPX6 jet tests, which stress a seal completely differently than static immersion does (a jet applies concentrated, directional pressure at a point, where immersion applies uniform pressure over the whole surface). “Waterproof” isn’t a specific enough term for an engineering spec because it doesn’t map to any single test; state the actual environmental exposure the product needs to survive, and select the corresponding IP digits or standards for each one. A product that sees both immersion and jets in service needs both requirements verified, not one used as a proxy for the other.


Are NEMA and IP ratings equivalent?


No. They’re distinct classification systems built around different concerns, and the relationship between them only runs one direction. NEMA 250 folds in environmental factors an IP code doesn’t touch at all, including corrosion resistance, icing, and oil exposure depending on enclosure type. A given NEMA type can meet or exceed what a comparable IP code requires, but an IP-rated enclosure can’t be assumed to satisfy the matching NEMA type just because a comparison chart lines them up next to each other, always verify against the actual NEMA requirements rather than treating the two codes as interchangeable shorthand.


How do you verify or certify an IP67 enclosure?


Verification means testing the defined configuration against IEC 60529, using an accredited lab where independent qualification is required. Records should identify the enclosure revision, seals, penetrations, connectors, covers, and other features affecting the environmental boundary. Production control then keeps subsequent units within that validated configuration. Any later design change affecting the boundary should trigger a review of whether the existing test evidence remains valid, with the decision recorded before the revision enters production.
